latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Total circulating plus sequestered asexual P. falciparum biomass in erythrocytes. It drives fever, hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, metabolic stress, and the substrate for microvascular sequestration; it is the main direct target of rapidly acting artemisinin therapy.

Mature infected erythrocytes adhere to endothelium and rosette with uninfected erythrocytes, hiding from peripheral smear and obstructing capillary beds in brain, lung, kidney, gut, placenta, and other organs.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Intravascular and extravascular hemolysis with splenic clearance
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Rupture of infected erythrocytes and accelerated clearance of infected and uninfected erythrocytes produce anemia, jaundice, high LDH, reticulocytosis, low haptoglobin, dark urine, and severe anemia physiology.

Hemozoin, parasite DNA, and rupture-cycle antigens activate monocytes, endothelium, and cytokine pathways, producing high fever, rigors, malaise, CRP/ferritin rise, capillary leak amplification, and sepsis-like physiology.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Endothelial activation and systemic capillary leak
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Microvascular inflammation and sequestration activate endothelium, impair nitric oxide signaling, increase permeability, and produce hypotension, hypoalbuminemia, pulmonary edema tendency, and organ hypoperfusion.

Brain microvascular sequestration, endothelial activation, impaired perfusion, acidosis, fever, seizure activity, and sometimes hypoglycemia combine to produce impaired consciousness, seizure, coma, and cerebral malaria hazard.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Renal microcirculatory, tubular, and pigment injury
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Renal capillary sequestration, hemoglobinuria, hypovolemia, acidosis, and tubular injury produce oliguria, rising creatinine/BUN, electrolyte disturbance, and severe AKI requiring renal replacement therapy.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Malaria-associated pulmonary capillary leak and ARDS
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Pulmonary endothelial activation, parasite antigen-driven inflammation, hypoalbuminemia, and fluid sensitivity produce non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema or ARDS, sometimes after peripheral parasitemia has cleared.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Severe malaria metabolic stress, acidosis, and hypoglycemia
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Parasite glucose consumption, impaired hepatic gluconeogenesis, quinine-related insulin release, anaerobic metabolism, renal failure, and shock drive hypoglycemia, hyperlactatemia, metabolic acidosis, and rapid mortality risk.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Falciparum gametocyte carriage and transmission potential
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Mature sexual-stage parasites that do not usually drive acute organ failure but matter for onward transmission and are targeted by single low-dose primaquine when safe.

supportive_care: Obtain thick and thin smears or rapid diagnostic testing urgently, repeat smears until parasite clearance, and do not wait for species confirmation when severe malaria is strongly suspected and testing is delayed.
Start rapid effective antimalarial therapy for severe manifestations and arrange full oral follow-on blood-stage therapy once parasite density and enteral status allow.
Monitor glucose at presentation and repeatedly during the first 24-48 hours, especially with coma, pregnancy, quinine exposure, liver dysfunction, poor intake, or renal failure.
Trend hemoglobin, reticulocytes, bilirubin, LDH, haptoglobin, and platelet count; transfuse red cells when severe anemia limits oxygen delivery or causes symptoms.
Monitor creatinine, BUN, potassium, bicarbonate, lactate, urine output, and acid-base status; involve nephrology early for oliguria, severe acidosis, hyperkalemia, uremia, or fluid overload.
Use cautious fluids: correct clear hypovolemia but avoid liberal crystalloid loading in adults with severe malaria because capillary leak and hypoalbuminemia can precipitate pulmonary edema.
For ARDS, use oxygen escalation, lung-protective ventilation, prone positioning when appropriate, conservative fluid strategy after perfusion is restored, and early ICU involvement.

For impaired consciousness or seizure, protect airway, check glucose immediately, treat seizures, avoid aspiration, and reassess for bacterial meningitis or other coma mimics when clinical data conflict.

Avoid routine corticosteroids for cerebral malaria or uncomplicated ARDS; reserve immune-modulating decisions for separate diagnoses or refractory late organizing lung injury after infection is controlled.
Do not model exchange transfusion as a routine outcome-improving intervention; current practical management emphasizes rapid antimalarial therapy and organ support.
Assess pregnancy, G6PD status, region of acquisition, prior prophylaxis, and possible drug resistance before selecting oral follow-on and transmission-blocking therapy.
After IV artesunate, monitor weekly for delayed hemolysis for several weeks when parasite density was high or hemolysis persists.
